overview: The Zulu kingdom grew out of the political transformations of southern Africa around the turn of the nineteenth century. Shaka’s reign began in 1816. Its history includes farmers, herders, families and artists as well as soldiers. The later Zululand entry crosses the British conquest and colonial administration.

periods.title: Before the expanded kingdom
periods.summary: The map begins before Shaka’s reign, during an era of growing chiefdoms and regional competition.

periods.title: The Zulu kingdom
periods.summary: Successive kings governed a powerful kingdom; Britain invaded in 1879.

periods.title: Conquest and colonial Zululand
periods.summary: Partition and conflict followed defeat. Britain annexed Zululand in 1887; it was incorporated into Natal in 1897.

items.text: Zulu state-building drew on cattle wealth, alliances and military organization. Shaka ruled from 1816 to 1828, but the regional changes had begun earlier. The map’s 1783 label should not turn his later kingdom into a fully formed eighteenth-century state.

British officials wanted to bring Zululand into a larger colonial federation. King Cetshwayo rejected demands that would surrender his authority and dismantle his army. British forces invaded in January 1879.

Zulu forces defeated the British at Isandlwana in January 1879, but a renewed invasion ended in defeat at Ulundi that July. Cetshwayo’s attempts to negotiate peace did not prevent the second British advance.

Conquest did not bring a simple peace. British partition helped produce further struggles over authority and land; formal annexation came in 1887. Colonial administration was partly financed through a hut tax, bringing imperial rule directly into household budgets.

A characteristic Nguni homestead placed dwellings around a central cattle enclosure. The arrangement connected houses, family relationships and livestock in one working space. Architectural studies describe regional conventions, not an identical plan followed by every Zulu family.

SAHO describes a household economy in which women cultivated grain and managed much domestic work, while men herded cattle, built structures and made tools and weapons. These linked tasks sustained communities and armies alike.

One Zulu wooden headrest in the British Museum was made before 1865. Its four long legs support an oval resting surface, darkened with pokerwork. It is 19 centimetres high: a carefully carved personal furnishing, not a modern fluffy pillow.

A spectacular nineteenth-century vessel at the Met was carved from one block of wood, with a separate lid and a surrounding four-legged support. It belongs to a group associated with Zulu-speaking carvers near Natal, including the named artist Unobadula.

Those carvers worked for local elites and European customers; examples appeared at London’s 1862 International Exhibition. The Met vessel’s original use remains uncertain: little wear and no detected residue caution against confidently calling it an everyday beer pot.

Locust damage in the 1890s and cattle diseases worsened the effects of colonial dispossession. More men sought wages on railways and mines. Families’ changing work patterns had political and environmental causes, not a sudden loss of agricultural knowledge.

A written isiZulu sample is “Ilanga lase Natal”, translated “The Natal Sun”. John Dube founded this newspaper in 1903. Its Latin-letter title is a real historical example of written isiZulu, from the colonial period rather than Shaka’s court.

Ilanga provided a space for African writers and political discussion. Its existence after conquest shows that Zulu-speaking people continued shaping public life through print as well as oral culture; losing an independent kingdom did not end their history.

ending.text: The independent kingdom was defeated in 1879, followed by partition, conflict, annexation in 1887 and incorporation into Natal in 1897. Zulu people, language and cultural institutions continued beyond the map’s 1914 endpoint.
